Parts E and F · Practice set

Practice set: vision, language and the world

Twenty-four questions on the seven chapters of Parts E and F, to attempt without notes

This practice set covers Parts E and F: how a vision transformer cuts a photo into patches, how CLIP learns from pairs of photos and captions, cross-attention by hand, the cost of image tokens and the projector of a vision-language model, fairness metrics at one threshold, re-identification, quantisation, the latency budget of a robot, and the whole SharkCam system. It mixes calculations that you do by hand, charts drawn from the data of the chapters, a short program to trace and statements to judge. Attempt it without notes and with the chapters closed. A timer is there if you want the pressure of a clock, and about an hour and a quarter is a fair target.

When you press Score my answers at the end, the page shows your score by area and the questions you missed, with links to the sections to revise. It does not show the correct answers. Revise the sections the score points to, try the missed questions again, and attempt the whole set again after a week.

You will need: a pen, paper and a calculator with exp, ln and square-root keys, and what Parts E and F teach: E1 Vision transformers and image tokens, E2 Encoders and CLIP, E3 Cross-attention, E4 Vision-language models, F1 Data, fairness and privacy, F2 AI on a robot and F3 SharkCam, end to end. Some questions use the dot product and cosine of 0.5, the softmax and the logarithms of 0.7, and the attention of D4.

How to use this set

  • Close the chapters. Keep a pen, paper and a calculator beside you.
  • Choose a time and press Start timer when you begin. Pause it when you leave. The clock counts down, then goes on counting past zero so that you can see how long you took. The timer is optional.
  • Skip a question and return to it if you like. Your answers are saved in this browser as you type.
  • Press Score my answers at the end. The set is scored only then.
Time allowed

Your answers and the timer are saved in this browser only. No data is sent anywhere.

Patches, tokens and position in a vision transformer

Question 1Patches, tokens and position in a vision transformer

SharkCam gives a vision transformer a square photo of 256 by 256 pixels. The model adds one class token to the patches (chapter E1). One attention head in one layer scores all pairs of tokens, so a sequence of \(n\) tokens gives \(n^2\) pairs. With a patch side of 32 pixels the head scores some number of pairs. The designers now change the patch side to 16 pixels. About how many times as many pairs does one head score? Give the ratio to one decimal place.

Revise E1 Cutting a photo into patches.

Question 2Patches, tokens and position in a vision transformer

The program in the figure cuts a wide photo into patches in the way of chapter E1. What does it print?

A made-up program. The photo is a block of zeros, 96 high and 160 wide with three colours, so only the sizes matter.

import numpy as np
H, W, P = 96, 160, 32
img = np.zeros((H, W, 3))
g = img.reshape(H // P, P, W // P, P, 3)
g = g.transpose(0, 2, 1, 3, 4)
patches = g.reshape(-1, P * P * 3)
print(patches.shape)
Choose one answer

Revise E1 Cutting a photo into patches.

Contrastive loss and zero-shot classification

Question 4Contrastive loss and zero-shot classification

To get the loss of one row, CLIP divides the row by the temperature \(T\) and takes the softmax over the three captions. The loss is the negative natural logarithm of the probability of the true caption. With \(T = 0.1\), what is the loss of the row of photo 2? Give three decimal places.

Cross-attention by hand and its cost

Question 8Cross-attention by hand and its cost

A captioning model has written “a hammerhead with a tall” and now writes “fin”. In cross-attention (chapter E3) the query comes from the words, and the keys and values come from three patches of the photo. The table gives the keys and values of one head and the query of “fin”. There is no mask. What is the second number of the output vector that the word receives? Give two decimal places.

Made-up numbers for one head. The query of the word “fin” is (2, 1), and \(d_k = 2\).

PatchKeyValue
Patch 1: water(−1, 1)(1, 2)
Patch 2: fin(1, 2)(0, 4)
Patch 3: body(2, −1)(3, −1)

Question 9Cross-attention by hand and its cost

A photo of 256 by 256 pixels is cut into patches of 16 by 16 pixels. The caption has \(n = 9\) words. Count pairs of a query and a key for one head in one layer (chapter E3). In design X the words read the \(N\) image tokens by cross-attention and read one another with the causal mask. In design Y the \(N\) image tokens are placed in front of the words in one sequence. They read one another in both directions, and the words read the image tokens and the earlier words. About how many times as many pairs does design Y compute as design X? Give the ratio to one decimal place.

Revise E3 What the image costs.

What attention maps show and do not show

Question 10What attention maps show and do not show

Chapter E3 hides patches of a photo and measures how much the log probability of a caption word falls. Three rules choose \(k\) patches to hide. The first takes the patches with the most attention weight, with the empty patches set aside. The second takes the patches that mattered most when hidden alone (the single-patch test). The third takes random patches. The charts show two words. Which statement do they support?

BLIP, two words of the captions of chapter E3. Coral is the k patches with the most attention weight (empty patches set aside), teal the k best patches of the single-patch test and navy k random patches. The fall is the drop in the log probability of the word, so a larger fall means the hidden patches mattered more (data file of chapter E3).

Choose one answer

Revise E3 Does the map show what matters?.

Where the numbers come from

  1. The charts and tables of questions 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 14, 15 and 20 are read from the data files of the chapters: e1-vision-transformers/data/shuffle.json (question 3), e2-clip/data/clip.json (5, 6 and 7), e3-cross-attention/data/occ.json (10), e4-vlms/data/vlm2.json (14), f1-fairness/data/clinic.json (15) and f2-robots/data/quant.json (20).
  2. The networks behind them are the torchvision ViT-B/16 and ResNet-18 (question 3) and CLIP ViT-B/32 of OpenAI (5, 6 and 7). They are also BLIP image captioning of Salesforce (10; BSD-3-Clause licence) and Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct (14; Apache-2.0 licence). Question 15 uses a logistic regression on the Pima women, and question 20 uses the digit reader of chapter C2. The Pima data is a published dataset of 768 women of Pima heritage, measured in the United States, and not data from Mumbai.
  3. Many numbers are invented for practice. These are the program of question 2 and the cosines of question 4. They are also the keys and values of question 8, the sizes of questions 9, 11, 12 and 13, and the base rates and rates of question 16. The table of patients of question 17 is invented.
  4. The layer and the weight of question 18 are invented. So are the stage times, the computer and the shark of question 19, the models and limits of question 21, and the chances of question 22. The problems of questions 23 and 24 are invented, and the 92% of question 24 is the example of chapter F3. The photo size in question 1 is a made-up size.
  5. The script data/make_tables.py reproduces the chart data. The solutions to all questions are kept apart from this page.
  6. The ideas come from chapters E1 to F3, listed at the top of this page.
